'''Raymond Julien Joseph Laflamme''', {{Post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|FRSC|size=95%}} ({{IPA|fr|ʁɛmɔ̃ ʒyljɛ̃ ʒozɛf laflam|lang}}; July 19, 1960 – June 19, 2025) was a Canadian [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] who was the founder and, until June 2017, the director of the [[Institute for Quantum Computing]] at the [[University of Waterloo]]. He was also a professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Waterloo and an associate faculty member at [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]]. Laflamme was a [[Canada Research Chair]] in Quantum Information. In December 2017, he was named as one of the appointees to the [[Order of Canada]].

As [[Stephen Hawking]]'s PhD student, he first became famous for convincing Hawking that time does not reverse in a contracting universe, along with [[Don Page (physicist)|Don Page]]. Hawking told the story of how this happened in his famous book ''[[A Brief History of Time]]'' in the chapter ''[[A Brief History of Time#Chapter 9: The Arrow of Time|The Arrow of Time]]''.<ref name="arrow of time" /> Later on, Laflamme made a name for himself in [[quantum computing]] and [[Quantum information|quantum information theory]], which was what he later became famous for. In 2005, Laflamme's research group created the world's largest [[Quantum computing#Quantum information processing|quantum information processor]] with 12 qubits.<ref>{{cite web |date=March 14, 2012 |title=Dr. Raymond Laflamme: Master of the quantum dance |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/science/research/research-stories/dr-raymond-laflamme |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180709095724/https://uwaterloo.ca/science/research/research-stories/dr-raymond-laflamme |archive-date=July 9, 2018 |access-date=January 4, 2013 |work=Science}}</ref> Along with Phillip Kaye and [[Michele Mosca]], he published the book ''An Introduction to Quantum Computing'' in 2006.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kaye |first1=Phillip |url=https://www.oupcanada.com/catalog/9780198570004.html |title=An Introduction to Quantum Computing |last2=Laflamme |first2=Raymond |last3=Mosca |first3=Michele |date=November 12, 2006 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780198570004 |access-date=January 4, 2013}}</ref> In 2024, he published the book ''Building Quantum Computers'' with Shayan Majidy and Christopher Wilson.<ref>
{{cite book |last1=Majidy |first1=Shayan |url=https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/building-quantum-computers/6A73C509D3E0F5F0A566A11F6A566A90 |title=Building Quantum Computers |last2=Wilson |first2=Christopher |last3=Laflamme |first3=Raymond |date=September 30, 2024 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781009417013}}
</ref>

Laflamme's research focused on understanding the impact of manipulating information using the laws of [[quantum mechanics]], the development of methods to protect [[quantum information]] against noise through [[quantum control]] and [[quantum error correction]] for [[quantum computing]] and [[Quantum cryptography|cryptography]], the implementation of ideas and concepts of [[quantum information science|quantum information processing]] using [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] to develop scalable methods of control of [[quantum systems]], and the development of blueprints for quantum information processors such as [[linear optical quantum computing]].<ref name="IQC profile"/>

==Biography==
Raymond Julien Joseph Laflamme was born on July 19, 1960, in [[Quebec City]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Erb & Good Funeral Home |date=June 19, 2025 |title=Raymond Julien Joseph Laflamme – 2025 |url=https://www.tributearchive.com/obituaries/43028876/raymond-julien-joseph-laflamme |access-date=June 22, 2025 |website=Tribute Archive}}</ref> to a medical doctor father and a dietician mother. He finished his undergraduate education at the [[Université Laval]] in Canada and went on to study at the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics at the [[University of Cambridge]], where he received the [[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos]] degree in 1984.<ref name="IQC profile">{{cite web |title=IQC People: Raymond Laflamme |url=https://services.iqc.uwaterloo.ca/people/profile/laflamme/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210902142612/https://services.iqc.uwaterloo.ca/people/profile/laflamme/ |archive-date=September 2, 2021 |access-date=January 4, 2013 |work=Institute for Quantum Computing}}</ref> Subsequently, his PhD supervisor was [[Stephen Hawking]]. Hawking mentioned in his book ''[[A Brief History of Time]]'' that Laflamme and [[Don Page (physicist)|Don Page]] were responsible for convincing him that time does not reverse in a contracting universe.<ref name="arrow of time">{{cite web |title=From correcting errors to building quantum computers |url=https://www.scientific-computing.com/feature/correcting-errors-building-quantum-computers |access-date=February 28, 2012 |website=Scientific Computing World}}</ref><ref name="uwaterloo.ca1">{{cite web |last=Grant |first=Matthew |date=September 14, 2017 |title=New research chair in quantum error correction – Institute for Quantum Computing |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/news/new-research-chair-quantum-error-correction |access-date=March 23, 2018 |website=University of Waterloo}}</ref> Hawking inscribed a copy of the book as follows: "To Raymond, who showed me that the arrow of time is not a boomerang. Thank you for all your help. Stephen."<ref>{{cite web |last=Laflamme |first=Raymond |date=January 8, 2012 |title=My time with Stephen Hawking |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/life/facts-and-arguments/my-time-with-stephen-hawking/article4085631/ |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241225064633/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/life/facts-and-arguments/my-time-with-stephen-hawking/article4085631/ |archive-date=December 25, 2024 |access-date=March 23, 2018 |work=[[The Globe and Mail]]}}</ref>

After completing his PhD,<ref name="uwaterloo.ca1"/> Laflamme worked as a Killam Postdoctoral Fellow at the [[University of British Columbia]] and in 1990, moved back to Cambridge as a Research Fellow at [[Peterhouse, Cambridge]].<ref name="IQC profile" /> Laflamme subsequently joined the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] where he was an Oppenheimer Fellow.<ref name="uwaterloo.ca2">{{cite web |date=September 14, 2017 |title=New research chair in quantum error correction demonstrates continued leadership by IQC and Waterloo in the pursuit of a quantum computer and in the development of other quantum technologies |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/news/news/new-research-chair-quantum-error-correction-demonstrates |access-date=March 23, 2018 |website=University of Waterloo}}</ref> In 1998, [[quantum teleportation]], including his work demonstrating the protocol with [[Nuclear spin|nuclear spins]], was ranked amongst the Top Ten [[Breakthrough of the Year|Breakthroughs of the Year]] by the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bloom |first=Floyd E. |author-link=Floyd E. Bloom |date=December 18, 1998 |title=Breakthroughs 1998 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.282.5397.2193 |journal=Science |volume=282 |pages=2193 |bibcode=1998Sci...282.2193B |doi=10.1126/science.282.5397.2193 |number=5397|url-access=subscription }} Among the cited works was {{cite journal |last1=Nielsen |first1=M. A. |last2=Knill |first2=E. |last3=Laflamme |first3=R. |date=November 5, 1998 |title=Complete quantum teleportation using nuclear magnetic resonance |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/23891 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=396 |issue=6706 |pages=52–55 |arxiv=quant-ph/9811020 |bibcode=1998Natur.396...52N |doi=10.1038/23891}}</ref> In 2001, he joined the newly founded [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]] and the Physics and Astronomy department of the affiliated [[University of Waterloo]], where he founded the [[Institute for Quantum Computing]] in 2002.<ref name="IQC profile"/>

In 2003, he became director of the Quantum Information program at the [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]]; he was also the scientific director of QuantumWorks, Canada's national research consortium on quantum information science, and held the [[Canada Research Chair]] in Quantum Information.<ref>{{cite web |date=December 2011 |title=Raymond Laflamme named APS Fellow |url=https://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/News/In_The_Media/Raymond_Laflamme_named_APS_Fellow/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121031165320/http://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/News/In_The_Media/Raymond_Laflamme_named_APS_Fellow/ |archive-date=October 31, 2012 |access-date=February 28, 2012 |website=Perimeter Institute}}</ref>

In June 2017, Laflamme stepped down as director at the Institute for Quantum Computing<ref>{{cite web |date=June 28, 2017 |title=Laflamme celebrates 15 years at quantum frontier |url=https://insidetheperimeter.ca/15-years-quantum-frontier/ |access-date=March 23, 2018 |website=Perimeter Institute}}</ref> and in September 2017, he was appointed the [[John von Neumann]] Chair in Quantum Information at the University of Waterloo, continuing his research on error correction in quantum systems. Laflamme continued to hold a Canada Research Chair<ref>{{cite web |title=Canada Research Chair Chairholders – Raymond Laflamme |url=https://www.chairs-chaires.gc.ca/chairholders-titulaires/profile-eng.aspx?profileId=747 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230217132156/https://www.chairs-chaires.gc.ca/chairholders-titulaires/profile-eng.aspx?profileId=747 |archive-date=February 17, 2023 |access-date=January 4, 2013 |website=Canada Research Chairs}}</ref> and a position as Associate Faculty at Perimeter Institute.<ref>{{cite web |date=November 20, 2017 |title=Quantum information pioneer Raymond Laflamme takes on new Chair |url=https://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/news/quantum-information-pioneer-raymond-laflamme-takes-new-chair |access-date=March 23, 2018 |website=Perimeter Institute}}</ref><ref name="uwaterloo.ca2"/>

Laflamme died from cancer in [[Waterloo, Ontario]], on June 19, 2025, at the age of 64.<ref name="s620">{{cite web |date=June 21, 2025 |title=IQC and Waterloo mourn the loss of Raymond Laflamme |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/news/legacy-quantum-research-excellence |access-date=June 22, 2025 |website=University of Waterloo}}</ref><ref name="NatPost-obit">{{cite news |last1=Knight |first1=Chris |title=Raymond Laflamme, Canadian pioneer in quantum computing, has died |url=https://nationalpost.com/news/raymond-laflamme-canadian-pioneer-in-quantum-computing-has-died |access-date=June 25, 2025 |work=[[National Post]] |date=June 24, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=Obituary of Raymond Julien Joseph Laflamme |date=June 19, 2025 |work=erbgood.com |url=https://erbgood.com/tribute/details/17675/Raymond-Laflamme/obituary.html |access-date=June 21, 2025}}.</ref>

==Scientific work==
[[File:Raymond Laflamme 2014.png|thumb|Laflamme in 2014, giving a lecture about [[Born rule]]]]
While Laflamme started his career working in [[quantum gravity]] and [[Quantum cosmology|cosmology]], he was known as a pioneering scientist in [[Quantum information|quantum information theory]]. While at Los Alamos, Laflamme was involved with the experimental implementation of quantum information processing devices using [[nuclear magnetic resonance]].

Laflamme laid down the mathematical framework for [[Quantum error correction|quantum error-correcting codes]], which has since developed into a broad topic of research. With colleagues Cesar Miquel, [[Juan Pablo Paz]] and [[Wojciech H. Zurek]], he constructed the most compact quantum error correcting code.<ref>{{cite web |title=University of Waterloo Physics and Astronomy profile: Raymond Laflamme |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/physics-astronomy/people-profiles/raymond-laflamme |access-date=January 4, 2013 |website=University of Waterloo}}</ref>

Two of his important and highly cited works were concerned with the computational power of a restricted set of states or operations. In joint work with [[Emanuel Knill]], he defined a quantum computational model of [[one clean qubit]] (DQC1) where a [[Quantum logic gate#Universal quantum gates|universal set of quantum gates]] is available, but all but one qubit are in a maximally mixed state.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=E. |last1=Knill |first2=R. |last2=Laflamme |title=Power of one bit of quantum information |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=81 |pages=5672–5675 |date=1998 |issue=25 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.81.5672 |arxiv=quant-ph/9802037 |bibcode=1998PhRvL..81.5672K }}</ref> This model defines a [[complexity class]] which is thought to be intermediate between classical computation ([[BPP (complexity)|BPP]]) and full quantum computing ([[BQP]]): it can solve efficiently some problems that are thought to be classically hard, but believed to be strictly weaker than BQP.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Peter W. |last1=Shor |first2=Stephen P. |last2=Jordan |title=Estimating Jones polynomials is a complete problem for one clean qubit |journal=Quantum Information & Computation |volume=8 |issue=8&9 |date=2008 |pages=681–714 |doi= 10.26421/QIC8.8-9-1|arxiv=0707.2831}}</ref>

Together with Knill and [[Gerard J. Milburn]], he showed that [[linear optics]], together with [[Photon counting|photon-counting]] measurements and [[feed-forward]], allow for efficient [[Universal quantum computer|universal quantum computation]] when acting on a suitable multi-photon [[Fock state]] as initial state ([[KLM protocol]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Knill |first1=Emanuel |last2=Laflamme |first2=Raymond |last3=Milburn |first3=Gerard |title=A scheme for efficient quantum computation with linear optics |year=2001 |journal=Nature |volume=409 |pages=46–52 |doi=10.1038/35051009 |pmid=11343107 |issue=6816 |bibcode=2001Natur.409...46K |s2cid=4362012}}</ref> This was an important result for optics-based approaches to quantum computing since it obviates the need to implement direct photon-photon interactions and laid the foundations for [[Linear optical quantum computing]] and, as a restriction of the KLM-model, to [[boson sampling]].

According to [[Scopus]], Laflamme had an [[h-index]] of 59 as of July 2025, with over 200 articles in scientific journals cited more than 24,000 times.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Laflamme, Raymond – Author details |url=https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=56234046800&origin=recordpage |access-date=July 14, 2025 |website=Scopus}}</ref>

In a 2013 interview, Laflamme described the importance of his work as follows: "Quantum information is going to change your life. And the one of your kids. And the one of your grandkids. And this is what I want to see. And this is what I expect to see: before I pass away, I will see that this [[Bohr–Einstein debates#The quantum revolution|quantum revolution]] is in full swing."<ref>{{cite web |last=Olsen |first=Lisa |date=June 25, 2013 |title=Institute for Quantum Computing |url=https://www.therecord.com/community-story/3855521-institute-for-quantum-computing/ |access-date=March 23, 2018 |website=Waterloo Region Record}}</ref>

==Media appearances==
Laflamme was a featured scientist in the award-winning documentary, ''The Quantum Tamers'' which was presented by the Perimeter Institute and saw its Canadian premiere in October 2009 at the [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics#Quantum to Cosmos: Ideas for the Future festival|Quantum to Cosmos]] festival in [[Waterloo, Ontario]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Biddiscombe |first=Claire |date=October 21, 2009 |title=Quantum Tamers captures prize |url=https://www.iqc.ca/institute/news_fulltext.php?id=131 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100523201428/http://www.iqc.ca/institute/news_fulltext.php?id=131 |archive-date=May 23, 2010 |access-date=February 28, 2012 |website=University of Waterloo}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Quantum Tamers: Revealing our weird & wired future |url=https://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/outreach/teachers/multimedia-resources/quantum-tamers-revealing-our-weird-wired-future |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109170909/http://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/outreach/teachers/multimedia-resources/quantum-tamers-revealing-our-weird-wired-future |archive-date=January 9, 2019 |access-date=February 28, 2012 |website=Perimeter Institute}}</ref> Laflamme was also a participant in ''[[The Agenda|The Agenda With Steve Paikin]]'' discussion panel, "Wired 24/7", with [[Neil Gershenfeld]], [[Jaron Lanier]], [[Neal Stephenson]], and [[Tara Hunt]] which took place at the festival.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Agenda With Steve Paikin: Wired 24/7 |url=http://www.q2cfestival.com/play.php?lecture_id=8012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100128231421/http://www.q2cfestival.com/play.php?lecture_id=8012 |archive-date=January 28, 2010 |access-date=February 28, 2012 |website=Quantum to Cosmos Festival}}</ref> The following year, Laflamme was a contributor at the 2010 [[TED (conference)|TEDx]] event, also in Waterloo, Ontario.<ref>{{cite web |date=February 25, 2010 |title=TEDxWaterloo 2010 |url=https://tedxwaterloo.com/event-details/february-2010/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414201244/http://tedxwaterloo.com/event-details/february-2010/ |archive-date=April 14, 2016 |access-date=January 4, 2013 |website=TEDxWaterloo}}</ref>

Laflamme was involved in several events surrounding the grand-opening of the [[Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre]] at the University of Waterloo. He was a participant at the "Bridging Worlds" panel discussion with Ivan Semeniuk, [[Mike Lazaridis]], [[Thomas Brzustowski]], and [[Chad Orzel]] at the Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre Open House in 2012.<ref>{{cite web |date=September 29, 2012 |title=Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre Open House |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/mike-ophelia-lazaridis-quantum-nano-centre/events/mike-ophelia-lazaridis-quantum-nano-centre-open-house |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304111620/https://uwaterloo.ca/mike-ophelia-lazaridis-quantum-nano-centre/events/mike-ophelia-lazaridis-quantum-nano-centre-open-house |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |access-date=January 4, 2013 |work=Mike & Ophelia Lazaridis Quantum-Nano Centre}}</ref>

As part of the grand-opening events, the [[Kitchener–Waterloo Symphony]] performed "Quantum: Music at the Frontier of Science" of which Laflamme was a collaborator in the creation of the concert narrative.<ref>{{cite web |last=Schnarr |first=Nancy |date=September 12, 2012 |title=The Kitchener-Waterloo Symphony Reboots Innovative Concert with Institute for Quantum Computing |url=https://kwsymphony.ca/media/releases/12-13quantum.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160311163829/http://kwsymphony.ca/media/releases/12-13quantum.pdf |archive-date=March 11, 2016 |access-date=January 4, 2013 |website=Kitchener–Waterloo Symphony}}</ref>

Laflamme appeared as a speaker at [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics#BrainSTEM: Your Future is Now|BrainSTEM: Your Future is Now]] festival which ran from September 30 to October 6, 2013.<ref>{{cite web |date=August 19, 2013 |title=Perimeter Institute Announces BrainSTEM: Your Future is Now Festival Schedule |url=https://www.exchangemagazine.com/morningpost/2013/week34/Monday/13081910.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170928215429/http://www.exchangemagazine.com/morningpost/2013/week34/Monday/13081910.htm#anchor |archive-date=September 28, 2017 |access-date=March 23, 2018 |website=Exchange Magazine}}</ref>
